summary: Describes TinyMT32, a pseudorandom number generator that produces 32-bit unsigned integers and is a small variant of the Mersenne Twister. Its small state suits embedded devices and it is simple and deterministic. It is not meant for cryptographic use.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a tiny dice-rolling machine that gives the same rolls from the same start, so two computers can follow along together. It is not safe for secrets.

questions: what is the tinymt32 parameter set
subtitle: A small, deterministic pseudorandom number generator whose output depends only on the seed, on any platform.

tldr.problem: Protocols that need both sender and receiver to compute the same pseudorandom sequence need a generator that is small enough for embedded devices and gives identical output for a given seed everywhere.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8682 fixes one parameter set for TinyMT32, a small variant of the Mersenne Twister with a 127-bit internal state, and gives a C reference implementation plus 50 check values for seed 1.
tldr.outcome: Any conforming implementation MUST produce the same output as the reference code, but the generator is not meant for cryptographic applications.

today: RFC 8682 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2020, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text names RFC 8681 as a specification that normatively depends on it.

sections.title: What TinyMT32 Is
sections.content:
TinyMT is a small-sized variant of the Mersenne Twister (MT) pseudorandom number generator introduced in 2011. RFC 8682 specifies the TinyMT32 variant, which outputs 32-bit unsigned integers, as a specialization of reference implementation version 1.1 (2015/04/24) by Mutsuo Saito and Makoto Matsumoto of Hiroshima University.

TinyMT is not meant to replace MT. Its period is far shorter, at 2^127 - 1, but its internal state is only 127 bits compared with 19937 bits for MT. Its outputs satisfy several statistical tests for non-cryptographic randomness, including BigCrush in TestU01 and AdaptiveCrush, and the RFC calls it a major improvement over the Park-Miller Linear Congruential generator specified in RFC 5170.

The RFC says that this determinism can be a key requirement, as with RFC 8681, which normatively depends on this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: TinyMT32 is a small cousin of a famous number-mixing machine. It is much smaller, so it fits in tiny gadgets, but it is still good at shuffling.

sections.title: The Fixed Parameter Set
sections.content:
TinyMT32 is initialized with a parameter set (mat1, mat2, tmat). The original implementation leaves it unspecified. To make the sequence depend only on the seed, this RFC says the following set MUST be used:

  • mat1 = 0x8f7011ee = 2406486510
  • mat2 = 0xfc78ff1f = 4235788063
  • tmat = 0x3793fdff = 932445695

This is the first entry of the precalculated parameter sets in tinymt32dc/tinymt32dc.0.1048576.txt by Kenji Rikitake, and the set used in his 2012 Erlang paper. A comment in the code notes that this set warrants that none of the 2^32 possible seeds leads to an all-zero 127-bit internal state, so the original period_certification() function was safely removed. A different parameter set would require reintroducing it.
sections.plainLanguage: The machine has three secret dials. The RFC sets them to one fixed position so every copy of the machine behaves the same.

sections.title: The Reference Implementation
sections.content:
Figure 1 reproduces the reference code, written in C for C99. It differs from the original source in several ways: the files tinymt32.h and tinymt32.c are merged, unused parts such as tinymt32_init_by_array() are removed, the parameter set is added to the initialization function, and code that depended on two's complement representation of negative integers was replaced by a more portable version.

The state is four 32-bit words (status[4]) plus the three parameters. tinymt32_init loads the seed and parameters, runs a mixing loop and then calls the state update PRE_LOOP = 8 times. tinymt32_generate_uint32 advances the state with tinymt32_next_state and returns the tempered result from tinymt32_temper. The two if (y & 1) and if (t1 & 1) branches replace the original negation tricks. The code comments note that they are more portable but may slow generation.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipe is short: stir the starting number with the dials a few times, then each time someone asks for a number, stir once more and hand over the result.

sections.title: Using the Generator
sections.content:
The PRNG MUST first be initialized with void tinymt32_init (tinymt32_t* s, uint32_t seed);. The seed is a 32-bit unsigned integer, and the value 0 is permitted. The caller allocates the tinymt32_t structure but leaves it uninitialized. Because each instance has its own structure, several instances can run in parallel.

Each time a new number is needed, the caller uses uint32_t tinymt32_generate_uint32 (tinymt32_t * s);, which returns a value between 0 and 2^32 - 1 inclusive. The caller must leave the structure unchanged between successive calls.

The RFC only outputs 32-bit values and does not map them to a smaller range, such as 10 to 49. A use case that needs a mapping must provide its own. If determinism is required, floating point should probably be avoided for the mapping because of rounding differences across platforms, and care should be taken not to introduce bias.
sections.plainLanguage: You wind up the machine once with a starting number, then press the button whenever you want a new number. Do not touch the insides between presses.

sections.title: Checking an Implementation
sections.content:
Any implementation in line with this specification MUST have the same output as the reference implementation in Figure 1. To increase confidence, the RFC lists the first 50 values returned by tinymt32_generate_uint32(s) with a seed of 1. They begin 2545341989, 981918433, 3715302833 and end with 2292524454. These come from the check32.out.txt file provided by the PRNG authors.

The determinism of the Figure 1 code was checked on high-end laptops running 64-bit Mac OS X and Linux/Ubuntu, a 32-bit ARM Cortex-A15 board, embedded cards with ARM Cortex-M0+, M3 or M4 microcontrollers, and low-end cards with a 16-bit TI MSP430 or an 8-bit Arduino ATMEGA2560, all those embedded ones running RIOT.
sections.plainLanguage: To prove your copy of the machine works, start it with the number 1 and compare the first 50 rolls with the answer sheet in the RFC.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content: The authors do not believe the specification generates specific security risks per se. However, the TinyMT and MT PRNGs must not be used for cryptographic applications. The abstract and introduction repeat this warning. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: This machine is fine for games and shuffling but never for guarding secrets, because someone clever could guess its next roll.
